entry.title: 19 Lines of Code: How I Won the Global Seam Miniapp Hackathon

link.title: 19 Lines of Code: How I Won the Global Seam Miniapp Hackathon

entry.content:
In the sweltering summer of 2024, I made a spontaneous decision to jump into the highly competitive Seam Miniapp Hackathon. The event attracted over a hundred brilliant software developers from across the globe, all vying for the top spot.

The prompt provided by the organizers carried a highly restrictive engineering constraint: we had to build an engaging, interactive web experience optimized to live natively inside the fast-paced, space-constrained ecosystem of social media comment sections. This wasn’t about building a sprawling web application; it was about designing a micro-experience that could capture a user’s attention in a fraction of a second.

Stage 1: The Global Culling (The Pull Request)

When brainstorming, my mind continuously drifted back to the late 90s and early 2000s—the nostalgic, chaotic era of flashing forum graphics, neon colors, and the raw energy of the HTML marquee text tags. I wanted to bring that retro, expressive energy into modern UI components with a customizable twist. I envisioned a lightweight tool where users could input simple text or emojis, set contrasting foreground/background colors, and watch their message cycle word-by-word like a rapid digital flipbook. I called it Dizzy Text.

The competition kicked off with a brutal first round. Stage 1 required us to submit our core concept and codebase via a GitHub Pull Request (PR). Over 100+ entries were submitted worldwide by talented engineering teams. I waited anxiously as the organizers vetted every single submission for code quality, architectural viability, and performance.

The validation was incredible: my PR was selected among the top 15–20 entries globally, securing my ticket to the final round.

The 48-Hour Sprint: Code-Golfing to 19 Lines

Moving into the finals, I gave myself a strict, non-negotiable 48-hour timeline to refine my conceptual prototype into a production-ready deployment.

The real engineering challenge wasn’t just building the application—it was shrinking it. To thrive inside a live comment section, my miniapp needed a near-zero rendering footprint. Any bloat or heavy external animation library would cause performance lag in the feed, ensuring instant rejection from the community.

I spent hours meticulously shaving off unnecessary dependencies, choosing to rely entirely on standard React primitives. By the end of day two, after intense code-golfing and refactoring, I successfully compressed the entire functional core of Dizzy Text into just 19 lines of pure React code.

The elegance lay in its simplicity. By blending useState and useEffect with a strategic use of the mathematical modulo operator (%), I created an infinite, responsive animation loop. This entirely eliminated the need for heavy state machines or complex CSS keyframe injections.

Stage 2: The Week-Long Voting Roller Coaster

Once the finalists were chosen, Stage 2 began. The organizers published our miniapps directly onto the live Seam website. This wasn’t a standard, passive voting page judged behind closed doors; it was a live test of market viability. To vote for an app, users in the community actively had to unlock the miniapp and interact with it directly inside their social comment feeds.

Watching the live leaderboard update over that week was an absolute emotional roller coaster. Because users were discovering and playing with the apps in real-time, the ranks shifted constantly:

  • Days 1–3: Dizzy Text immediately exploded in popularity. Users stopped typing boring text and started using my 19 lines of code to create rapid-fire emoji animations and flashing micro-stories. I captured 1st place.
  • Days 4–5: Competitors rallied their networks. I slipped to 2nd place, trading the top spot back and forth by mere fractions of percentage points.

Seeing the rank slip only fueled my commitment. I doubled down on engaging with the community, demonstrating creative use cases for the tool, and gathering live feedback.

Because of that relentless push, the word-of-mouth momentum became entirely unstoppable. By the final day, the adoption curve verticalized. I didn’t just win; I pulled ahead by a massive, undeniable margin.

Victory and Beyond

When the public voting officially concluded, Dizzy Text secured First Place globally, letting me proudly bring home the $500 grand prize.

Yet, looking back on the whirlwind experience, the true reward extended far beyond the title. Within mere days, Dizzy Text achieved viral community adoption, being actively unlocked and utilized by over 1,000 unique users across countless Seam posts.

This hackathon served as a powerful reminder for my broader software engineering career: you absolutely do not need thousands of lines of bloated, over-engineered code to make a massive, measurable impact on a user base. Sometimes, extreme optimization, a clear vision, and just 19 lines of highly refined logic is exactly what it takes to win.
entry.summary: How absolute code optimization, a multi-stage battle, and a strict 48-hour sprint turned my lightweight text component into a viral, hackathon-winning miniapp.

entry.title: Markets & Forecasting: How my passion lead to Google-backed KaggleX fellowship

link.title: Markets & Forecasting: How my passion lead to Google-backed KaggleX fellowship

entry.content:
In the summer of 2023, my deep-rooted passion for financial markets naturally drew me into the complex world of time-series forecasting. I started spending countless hours working on predictive models, fascinated by the idea of decoding hidden patterns within seemingly chaotic datasets. It was during this intense period of self-directed research and building that I decided to apply for the KaggleX BIPOC Fellowship.

I had actually applied to the previous cohort and faced a tough rejection. So, when the acceptance email finally arrived this time around, my excitement went through the roof. Based on the rigorous preliminary forecasting work I had been doing and the technical requirements of my ongoing projects, I was officially allotted the fellowship and awarded the prestigious $1,000 KaggleX Scholarship, backed by Google.

This program wasn’t merely an academic exercise; it was an intensive, mentorship-driven deep dive. Paired with an incredible mentor, Ayon Roy, I had the perfect environment to tackle a notoriously difficult challenge: mastering complex store sales forecasting.

The Problem: The Chaos of Retail Data

Forecasting retail sales is a problem that sits at the volatile intersection of human behavior, macroeconomics, and temporal cycles. Unlike stationary datasets where patterns remain relatively consistent over time, store sales data is inherently chaotic. It is heavily influenced by overlapping seasonal trends, sudden holiday sales spikes, localized promotional events, and random economic noise.

When I first began analyzing the historical data, it became immediately apparent that relying on a singular, standard machine learning algorithm would be insufficient. A simple linear regression model would completely miss the overarching macro-trends, while a basic tree-based model might overfit to the random noise, failing to generalize to future data points. To achieve elite predictive performance, I needed to push the boundaries of standard modeling and engineer a highly sophisticated, multi-layered solution.

The Architecture: A Hybrid Paradigm

The core philosophy driving my approach was the understanding that different machine learning algorithms possess distinctly different strengths. I spent several weeks conceptualizing a hybrid forecasting architecture that could leverage the unique advantages of two entirely distinct paradigms: classical time-series decomposition and modern gradient boosting.

The goal was to create a system where one model handled the broad, predictable strokes of the data, while a second model aggressively targeted the unpredictable, non-linear anomalies left behind.

Layer 1: Capturing the Macro with Prophet

For the foundation, I turned to Prophet, a robust forecasting procedure built for handling time-series data that displays strong seasonal effects and historical trend changes. I engineered the Python pipeline to utilize Prophet to capture the macro-level trends.

This involved carefully tuning the model to recognize multi-period seasonality, explicitly mapping out weekly shopping habits, monthly wage cycles, and yearly holiday patterns. By configuring Prophet to understand these underlying rhythms, I generated a baseline forecast—a highly accurate representation of what sales should look like in a perfectly predictable world.

Layer 2: Conquering the Residue with XGBoost

The real world, however, is never perfectly predictable. Prophet inherently struggles with sharp, sudden irregularities that occur in daily operations. This is where the second layer of the hybrid architecture was introduced.

I engineered the pipeline to isolate the statistical residue of the Prophet model—the exact mathematical difference between the smooth baseline prediction and the actual historical sales data. This residue represented everything the time-series model failed to understand: the chaotic noise, the impact of a sudden local competitor, or the unexpected success of a specific product promotion.

To conquer this residue, I deployed an XGBoost Regressor. Instead of training the XGBoost model on the raw sales figures, I trained it explicitly to learn and fit onto the error margin left behind by the first model. The algorithm essentially learned how to predict the mistakes of the Prophet baseline based on auxiliary features like daily oil prices, specific holiday flags, and localized promotional data.

The Engineering Sprint and Final Results

The engineering required to make these two systems work in tandem was the most demanding phase of the fellowship. I spent over a month writing Python scripts to iteratively tune the hyperparameters of both models simultaneously, ensuring they complemented rather than contradicted one another. I built robust data cleaning pipelines to handle missing values without breaking the strict chronological order required for time-series forecasting, and I implemented complex time-series cross-validation techniques to ensure the model was never inadvertently exposed to future data.

By layering the immense gradient-boosting power of XGBoost directly on top of Prophet’s seasonal baseline, I successfully created a framework that could see both the forest and the trees. It respected the overarching, macro-economic seasonal cycles while aggressively adapting to daily, micro-level anomalies.

When deployed against a complex, unseen testing dataset, the final hybrid model achieved an outstanding 87.8% predictive accuracy.

Beyond the raw metrics, the KaggleX Fellowship was a profound period of professional growth. Weekly touchpoints with my mentor forced me to constantly defend my architectural decisions, refine my code quality, and think about scalability. Collaborating with a global cohort of peers completely transformed my confidence as an engineer. It taught me that true engineering is about deeply understanding the underlying physics of your data, embracing its chaos, and orchestrating highly customized, complementary systems to win.

I use AI for proof-reading & grammar
entry.summary: How my passion for markets led to a Google-backed KaggleX Fellowship, and the hybrid time-series and gradient boosting architecture I built to achieve 87.8% accuracy.

entry.title: Edge AI: Engineering Local Image Classification on Android

link.title: Edge AI: Engineering Local Image Classification on Android

entry.content:
During my 4th year as an undergraduate student at IIT Bombay, I wanted to move beyond theoretical machine learning frameworks and tackle real-world mobile engineering constraints. This drive led me to join the SPANN Lab under the guidance of Prof. V.M. Gadre as an Android Developer through the iSURP IITB initiative.

My core objective was clear: bridge the gap between heavy machine learning models and mobile deployment architectures. I needed to build a production-ready application from scratch that could execute intelligent vision systems locally, completely bypassing the need for high-latency, cloud-based infrastructure.

The Challenge: Breaking Free from Cloud Latency

Traditional mobile applications typically offload computer vision tasks to remote servers via API endpoints. While this saves device memory, it introduces significant latency and makes the app completely dependent on continuous network connectivity.

To achieve zero-latency, on-device intelligence (Edge AI), the machine learning model had to run natively within the client environment on a standard smartphone chip. The real engineering bottleneck was figuring out how to execute this without draining the hardware’s resources or causing the UI to freeze during inference.

The Architecture: Bridging Java and Python

I started the pipeline by wireframing a modern, intuitive user interface in Figma to cleanly present the analytical data. Once the design system was locked in, I transitioned to Android Studio to build the core application framework using Java.

To solve the localized inference problem, I engineered a hybrid runtime architecture:

  • The Bridge: I integrated the Chaquopy SDK, a robust toolkit that allows seamless script execution and bidirectional communication between Java-based Android components and localized Python environments.
  • The Engine: Within the Python layer, I utilized the TensorFlow Lite (TFLite) module to load highly compressed, pre-trained image classification models optimized for mobile.
  • The Pipeline: I built a custom bitmap conversion pipeline. The Java frontend captured live camera frames, optimized their dimensions, and passed the raw byte arrays across the SDK bridge. The Python backend instantly processed the frames, executed the TFLite inference, and smoothly returned the classification tokens back to the UI.

The Result: Real-Time Edge Intelligence

The months spent refining this memory-conscious architecture paid off. I successfully delivered a highly optimized, fully functional system capable of real-time local image classification.

This project proved that hardware constraints on edge devices can be overcome with smart, cross-language software design. Beyond the technical milestones, this journey in full-stack mobile AI engineering was highly rewarding, capping off with a personal Letter of Recommendation from Prof. Gadre validating the rigorous approach.
entry.summary: How I built a zero-latency, on-device image classification Android app using Java, Python, and TFLite during my 4th year as an undergraduate at IIT Bombay.

entry.title: Scaling Mentorship: Earning Top Tutor at Coursehero

link.title: Scaling Mentorship: Earning Top Tutor at Coursehero

entry.content:
During my third year at IIT Bombay, I wanted a practical way to apply my passion for mathematics and problem-solving outside of my standard coursework. I decided to apply as a tutor on Coursehero (now part of Learneo) to see if I could effectively teach these concepts to others. What started as an experiment turned into a highly rewarding stint that lasted for almost a full year.

Starting in Electrical Engineering

I initially joined the platform strictly as an Electrical Engineering tutor. My goal was straightforward. I didn’t want to just hand out static answers. I wanted to break down complex, advanced engineering bottlenecks into logical steps that a student sitting anywhere in the world could easily follow.

Remote mentoring is uniquely challenging because you have to diagnose exactly where a student is stuck purely through text and digital equations. I put a lot of effort into making my explanations as clear and fundamentally sound as possible. That practical approach paid off quickly, and I managed to maintain a flawless 100% helpful rate for several consecutive months.

Upgrading and Expanding Domains

Because of that consistent positive response and effort, the Coursehero core team took notice. They directly connected with me and upgraded my profile, unlocking a much wider range of subjects. I went from exclusively handling EE questions to actively tutoring across Mathematics, Electrical Engineering, and Computer Science.

Over the course of the year, I systematically tackled over 200 advanced questions across these three domains. Maintaining high academic integrity and precision was my top priority, and even with the expanded workload, I held onto a 95% overall positive rating from the student community.

The Takeaway: Top Tutor Status and $3,000

The metrics by the end of my run were highly satisfying. I earned almost $3,000 USD over the year and was officially awarded the title of Top Tutor. More importantly, establishing a direct connection with the core team gave me a great inside look at how global EdTech platforms operate, evaluate talent, and scale their mentorship.

Eventually, I reached a point where I felt completely fulfilled with the role and what I had accomplished, so I decided to step away to focus on my next set of engineering challenges. Beyond the financial reward and the official badges, that year fundamentally sharpened my ability to communicate highly technical concepts with extreme clarity. That specific skill has proven to be incredibly useful for my broader career in engineering and software architecture.
entry.summary: A practical look back at my year tutoring on Coursehero, expanding from Electrical Engineering to CS and Math, and earning Top Tutor status.

entry.title: Cracking GATE Electronics: How I Secured AIR 2 in My Third Year

link.title: Cracking GATE Electronics: How I Secured AIR 2 in My Third Year

entry.content:
The Graduate Aptitude Test in Engineering (GATE) is widely known as a highly competitive evaluation. It is not a test of simple formulas or rote memorization. Instead, it is a comprehensive three-hour exam designed to rigorously evaluate your grasp of core engineering concepts, applied mathematics, and analytical problem-solving.

Achieving a top rank in this exam was a incredibly rewarding milestone for me. Securing an All India Rank (AIR) 2 in the GATE Electronics paper during my third year at IIT Bombay, competing against more than 55,000 students across the country, validated a highly specific, disciplined strategy.

If you are a student preparing for this exam, especially while balancing a demanding college schedule, here is the practical blueprint and the exact methods I used to build that foundational knowledge.

1. Ditch Rote Memorization for NPTEL

When you are sitting in the examination hall, surface-level knowledge fails under the pressure of carefully designed, multi-layered questions. You simply cannot shortcut your way to a top rank.

My primary source of truth throughout my preparation was NPTEL. While many students find NPTEL lectures to be slow or mathematically dense, that exact depth is what you need to succeed. I used these lectures to completely immerse myself in the physics of semiconductors, the mathematics of signal processing, and the underlying logic of digital circuits. I approached the syllabus by deconstructing complex systems down to their first principles. When you learn from NPTEL, you learn why a formula works, not just how to plug numbers into it.

2. The Art of Structured Note-Taking

Watching lectures is passive learning, but engineering requires active execution. The true cornerstone of my preparation was my note-taking strategy.

As I watched the NPTEL content, I systematically distilled hours of dense academic theory into highly structured, actionable personal notes. These notes essentially became my customized textbooks. I categorized them meticulously by:

  • Core theoretical concepts
  • Mathematical derivations and proofs
  • Edge-case problem-solving frameworks

When the final months of revision arrived, I did not have to waste time re-watching videos or flipping through massive reference books. I relied entirely on these self-made notes, refining my speed and accuracy with every single revision cycle.

3. Balancing GATE Prep with Your Third Year

Managing high-intensity exam preparation while navigating your third year of an undergraduate degree is a massive balancing act. Between handling rigorous college semesters, lab submissions, and regular coursework at IIT Bombay, time was a highly constrained resource.

The key to surviving this workload was ruthless time management and smart scheduling. I treated my GATE preparation as a core course of its own, dedicating fixed, non-negotiable hours to it every week. Having my notes highly organized meant that even if I only had a brief 45-minute window between college lectures, I could immediately open a specific section and execute a targeted revision session without losing momentum.

The Takeaway

Preparing for GATE is a journey that shapes how you think as an engineer. The underlying philosophy required to conquer it involves breaking down massive, complex problems into elegant, manageable, and logically sound components.

Whether your ultimate goal is to pursue advanced research, secure a role in a top public sector enterprise, or build high-performance software systems, the mathematical resilience and disciplined learning habits you forge during your GATE preparation will serve as your most valuable engineering assets. Stick to the fundamentals, leverage NPTEL, build your own comprehensive notes, and trust the process.

My workflows involve using AI for writing/compiling my final thoughts
entry.summary: A practical preparation blueprint detailing how I leveraged NPTEL and structured notes to achieve AIR 2 in GATE Electronics during my third year at IIT Bombay.
